Confidence-Aware Tree-of-Thoughts:
A Federated Safety Net for VLM Agents in
Smart-Home Consumer Electronics
Tianle Zheng∗,†,¶, Heng Liu∗,¶, Lulu Xu∗, Junjie Wang∗, Yuxiang Zhang‡,∥, and Yiyao Yu∗,§
Abstract—Vision-language model (VLM) agents are entering
smart-home consumer electronics such as hubs, cameras and
connected appliances, where a single hallucinated action, for
example turning on a stove mistaken for a microwave, can
cause damage or a safety incident. Across five open-weight
VLMs from four families (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, Phi-
3.5-Vision, PaliGemma) and three parameter scales (3B, 4B,
7B), zero-shot accuracy with two-shot text prompts stays below
73% on our test splits. This paper makes four contributions.
First, we build SmartHome-VSV, a benchmark of 22,841 training
samples and three test splits (GQA-test, HARD-CONF, ADE-
CONF) auto-derived from public scene graphs with no human
annotation. Second, we propose a Confidence-Aware Selective
Tree-of-Thoughts verifier with three branches, a JSON five-tuple
verdict (C), a full-image yes/no detector (A) and a bounding-
box yes/no detector (B), trained jointly by multi-task LoRA
so that a soft threshold on the single-token logprobs of A
and B routes the final decision. Third, we deploy the verifier
under FFA-LoRA federated fine-tuning across three non-IID
households and confirm that aggregation is exact to machine
precision. Fourth, the same mechanism reduces dangerous error
by only 2.8 percentage points under centralized training, yet
recovers 28.2 points (37% relative) under federated drift, a ten-
fold amplification. Threshold sweeps, calibration analysis across
all backbones, branch ablations, bootstrap confidence intervals,
latency measurements and robustness tests show that the gain is
statistically reliable and adds only about 4% inference latency.
Confidence-Aware Selective ToT therefore acts as a distributional-
robustness safety net for federated generative AI on consumer
devices.
Index Terms—Vision-language models, smart-home consumer
electronics, federated learning, tree-of-thoughts, safety verifica-
tion.

sections.heading: Confidence routing.
sections.text: A verification module is only as useful as its calibration: when the underlying classifier is overconfident, hard-threshold gating provides little safety benefit. Our pipeline handles all four in one design (Fig. 1). Three branches are trained jointly on auto-derived data. Branch C emits a JSON five-tuple safety verdict, branch A asks “is there a ⟨ target ⟩ visible in this image?” on the full frame, and branch B asks “is this region clearly a ⟨ target ⟩ ?” on the bbox crop returned by C. A and B are trained to emit one token ( yes or no ), which lets us read well-calibrated probabilities P A , P B from the logprob of that position. Verification is then a soft- threshold problem rather than a hand-tuned cascade. We then run this verifier inside a five-round FFA-LoRA [13] federated protocol with three non-IID household clients. FFA- LoRA freezes the LoRA factor A across clients and trains only B . Because the frozen A is identical across clients, aggregating ¯ B = � i ( n i /N ) B i recovers an exact FedAvg of the parameter delta ∆ W = BA [14], a property we verify to machine precision across all five rounds (Section V). The protocol is illustrated in Fig. 2. The main finding appears when the verifier runs inside the federated protocol. On a centrally trained VLM, Confidence- Aware ToT reduces aggregate dangerous error on the three test splits by a modest 2.8 points; the centralized branch C is already accurate enough that A and B are largely redundant. Under non-IID federation, the average branch C verifier nearly collapses on the confusable-object subsets (ag- gregate dangerous error rises from 19 . 3% to 76 . 1% ), because no single client has seen the full vocabulary of household appliances. The same A and B branches that were dormant under centralized training now veto most of these dangerous executions, recovering 28.2 points of safety, a 37% relative reduction and a roughly tenfold amplification of the centralized gain. Confidence-Aware Selective ToT is therefore best read as a distributional robustness mechanism. It is precisely the federated non-IID regime mandated for privacy-preserving consumer electronics [11], [12], [15] that pays the largest safety dividend. Contributions: •

R ELATED W ORK A. VLMs for consumer devices and on-device GenAI The IEEE TCE community has recently devoted significant attention to deploying generative models on consumer hard- ware. Wu et al. [8] survey advances in AI-enabled vehicular edge computing for consumer electronics; Gupta et al. [7] design a privacy-preserving route optimization protocol for consumer vehicular networks. Although these works target vehicles, the same constraints of bounded memory, privacy and low-latency verification apply directly to smart-home VLM agents. Beyond passive perception, vision-language- action models now close the loop from pixels to actuation: VLA-Adapter shows that a tiny-scale bridge module lets sub- billion-parameter backbones drive robotic actions competi- tively [5], and Orca couples a VLA policy with an internal world model for long-horizon embodied tasks [6]. These systems strengthen the case for on-device action-emitting VLMs, and simultaneously widen the attack surface that our verify-before-act safety net addresses. Our target is a VLM as small as 3B parameters that can run on a typical hub-class accelerator. B. Federated learning for consumer electronics Kumar et al. [11] couple federated learning with blockchain auditing to preserve privacy in consumer electronics applica- tions; He et al. [12] combine federated meta-learning with dig- ital twins for intrusion detection on 6G-enabled consumer de- vices; Yang et al. [15] apply graph neural learning to anomaly detection in SDN-enabled consumer electronics. We federate a generative VLM verifier rather than a low-rank classifier, a setting in which the LoRA aggregation discrepancy [13] becomes a central concern. We adopt FFA-LoRA [13] for exact aggregation; standard FedAvg [14] and its heterogeneous variants [16], [17] underlie our protocol. C. Tree of Thoughts and verifier-style reasoning Tree of Thoughts [9] and ReAct [10] introduced multi-step reasoning over text. A parallel line of work pairs tree search with neural value estimation in structured decision domains: neural Monte Carlo Tree Search has been applied to first-order semantic games [18] and quantified Boolean formula satisfac- tion [19]. These lines motivate routing among multiple neural checks instead of trusting a single autoregressive verdict. Our verifier reuses the structural insight of multiple parallel checks before action but specializes it for VLM safety: we use the bbox returned by the JSON branch to route a cropped second- look verification, and we keep the checks at a single token so that calibration is well defined. Training data are auto-derived from public scene graphs into three task families (C: 5-tuple JSON; A: full-image yes/no; B: bbox-crop yes/no). A single multi-task LoRA adapter (rank 64) is fine-tuned on a frozen VLM. At inference time, branch C produces the primary 5-tuple verdict; branch A emits a single-token detection over the full image; branch B is invoked only when C’s bbox exceeds 5% of the image area. The final action is gated by a soft-threshold rule on the logprobs of A and B. D. VLM hallucination evaluation and trustworthy visual de- cision making POPE [20] and OPERA [21] evaluate object hallucination in VLMs. Our task differs in two important ways: (i) we measure action-level dangerous errors, not just object-level hallucina- tions, and (ii) we provide a complete benchmark including refuse-with-reason labels grounded in scene-graph attributes. A complementary line of work builds trustworthy visual rec- ognizers whose confidence is itself a first-class output. TMFF fuses multi-focus evidence with explicit uncertainty for multi- label sewer defect classification [22], PipeCLIP conditions a vision-language model on defect priors and cross-focus cues for video-based sewer inspection [23], and human-object- interaction-aware emotion recognition exposes trustworthy emotion states from a VLM [24]. Our verifier shares their design principle, multiple complementary evidence branches fused under calibrated confidence, but applies it to action gating on consumer devices, where a miscalibrated “yes” directly actuates hardware. Training-free safety wrappers are also relevant: prompt based alignment, self-reflection [25] and multi-agent debate [26] improve output quality without touching the weights; we compare against a self-reflection baseline in Section VI-G. E. LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning LoRA [27] parameterizes ∆ W = BA with low-rank A, B . FFA-LoRA [13] freezes A to recover exact FedAvg semantics. We adopt FFA-LoRA for the federated experiment and stan- dard LoRA for the centralized baseline; in both cases we attach rank-64 adapters to the { q, k, v, o, gate , up , down } projections and keep all pre-trained weights, including the vision tower, frozen. F. Adjacent deep learning deployment contexts The concerns that motivate our verifier (safety, robustness and domain adaptation of large neural models) recur across a broader set of specialized deployments. Differentiable safety- critical control has been used for adaptive quadruped loco- motion [28], and robust representation learning for virtual- machine-protected code [29]; both target the same do-no-harm objective that guides our verify-before-act pipeline. In vision, self-supervised large vision models have been extended to structural biology density maps [30], and vector-quantized generative modeling has been used for co-speech gesture synthesis [31], showing the cross-domain transfer of VLM training recipes. Consumer biosignal deployments raise related on-device requirements: transformer architectures have been adapted for SSVEP-based brain–computer interfaces [32], and clinical deep learning pipelines for body composition analysis in cardiometabolic disorders [33]. sections.text: ENCHMARK A. Task: verify-before-act Each example is a tuple ( I, a, c ) where I is a household image, a is a proposed action verb ( turn_on , turn_off , . . . ), and c is the target object class. The verifier must emit a 5-tuple JSON: � label , evidence bbox , pre state , post state , reason � . The label is one of EXECUTE , REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING , or REFUSE_STATE_CONFLICT . The bbox is required when the label is EXECUTE . B. Auto-derivation from scene graphs We construct training and test sets entirely from pub- lic scene-graph datasets, with zero human annotation. From GQA [36] we extract object boxes, attributes, and inter-object relations; from ADE20K [37] we extract semantic segmen- tation maps that we convert to per-class bounding boxes. For each scene we synthesize candidate actions by drawing a target class c from a hand-curated smart-home appliance dictionary (16 classes). The full derivation procedure is deterministic and we document every rule below.

sections.heading: Action vocabulary and object mapping.
sections.text: The appli- ance dictionary contains 16 target classes (door, window, curtain, blind, fridge/refrigerator, microwave, oven, stove, light, lamp, television/tv, faucet, sink, toilet) mapped to 27 class-specific actions (26 of which occur in the de- rived data) through a fixed affordance table: open / close for door, window, curtain, blind, fridge and microwave; turn_on / turn_off for microwave, oven, stove, light, lamp, tv and faucet; and flush for toilet. Synonymous scene- graph names ( fridge / refrigerator , tv / television , sink / faucet ) share one affordance entry.

sections.heading: Label rules.
sections.text: (i) Absent target : if no instance of c appears in the scene graph, the label is REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING with reason object_class_ c _absent . Training negatives draw c uniformly at random from the absent affordance classes of each scene that contains at least one smart-home object; the confusable-sibling constraint described below is applied only when mining the CONF test splits, not during training, so the training distribution is not biased toward any particular sibling pair. (ii) State conflict : the pre-state of a present target is inferred from its scene-graph attributes ( open , closed , on , lit , off , dark ; otherwise unknown ); if the inferred pre- state already equals the post-state of the proposed action (e.g., open_window on a window whose attribute is open ), the label is REFUSE_STATE_CONFLICT . Unknown pre-states never generate conflicts. (iii) Execute : otherwise the label is EXECUTE ; every annotated instance of c yields a candidate tuple whose evidence bbox is that instance’s box, and scenes with two or more instances are diverted to the MULTI splits so that grounding ambiguity does not contaminate the main splits.

sections.heading: Confusable-sibling mining.
sections.text: The CONF test splits are re- stricted to scenes in which the target is absent but at least one class from a hand-written confusion table is present (television ↔ monitor/screen/laptop, stove ↔ oven/cooktop/range, fridge ↔ freezer, light ↔ lamp/chandelier, window ↔ mirror/frame, door ↔ doorway/archway, faucet ↔ tap/spout, curtain ↔ blind/drape, toilet ↔ urinal/bidet, and analogous entries for the remaining classes).

sections.heading: Manual
sections.text: label audit. Because the labels are derived rather than human-annotated, we manually audited a strat- ified sample of 40 examples (8 GQA-test EXECUTE , 6 REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING , 2 REFUSE_STATE_CONFLICT , 12 HARD-CONF, 12 ADE-CONF). 36 of 40 labels (90%) were visually correct. All four disagreements trace back to scene-graph granularity on confusable sibling pairs, e.g. a television annotated only as screen so that the derived label claims the television is absent, or a range annotated as stove so that oven is treated as missing. Such cases make the CONF dangerous-error rates slightly conservative (a correct refusal may be scored against a technically present sibling), and none of them affects the EXECUTE training targets except one mislocalized window box. We release the audit list with the benchmark. C. Splits We report results on three signal-bearing splits, each of 500 examples; their exact label composition is stated here because the dangerous-error denominator depends on it: •

Branch structure and prompts Given ( I, a, c ) , the three branches consume the following prompts (the vision token sequence is prepended in every case): C Proposed action: a (target object class: c ). Respond JSON. A Is there a c visible in this image? yes/no. B Is this region clearly a c ? yes/no. Branch C outputs the 5-tuple JSON; branches A and B output a single token. The bbox needed by B is taken from C’s output (the evidence bbox field) and the corresponding crop is padded by 10%, resized to at least 384 × 384 , and fed back to the same VLM. B. Multi-task LoRA training All three branches share a single LoRA adapter of rank r = 64 attached by module name to the { q, k, v, o, gate , up , down } projections; all pre-trained weights, including the vision tower, stay frozen. Because the match is by name, the adapter also covers the identically named projections inside the vision encoder (the MLP gate/up/down projections of the Qwen2.5- VL ViT and the attention q, k, v projections of SigLIP), which account for 12–29M of the trainable parameters in Table I; for Phi-3.5-V the fused qkv / gate_up projections of the language model are targeted.

sections.heading: Token-level details.
sections.text: The strings yes and no are single tokens in all four tokenizer families we use: ids 9693/2152 in the Qwen2 tokenizer shared by Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B and LLaVA- OneVision, 4874/694 in the Phi-3.5 SentencePiece tokenizer, and 3276/956 in the PaliGemma (Gemma) tokenizer. In prac- tice we read the top-20 log-probabilities at the single gen- eration position and aggregate the probability mass of every token whose decoded surface form starts with “yes” or “no” (covering case and leading-whitespace variants such as Yes or yes ), then renormalize over the two aggregates. Restricting the renormalization to the yes/no mass is justified empirically: because branches A and B are fine-tuned to emit exactly one of these two tokens, the yes/no aggregates dominate the top- 20 candidates; across all 17,464 logged evaluation records the extraction never fell back to the undefined case (which we flag whenever the combined yes/no mass drops below 10 − 6 ), i.e., a yes/no variant appears in the top-20 for 100% of samples. Section VI-E quantifies the resulting calibration with ECE, Brier scores and risk–coverage analysis. Three decision rules are then defined over the triple (ˆ y C , P A , P B ) :

sections.heading: Confidence-Aware.
sections.text: Replace the hard threshold of 0 . 5 in Smart v1 with τ = 0 . 7 . This soft threshold treats any moderately uncertain detection as a refuse signal. The motivation for τ = 0 . 7 is illustrated by Fig. 5: for both branches, the confidence distribution on ground-truth EXECUTE examples is sharply concentrated near 1 . 0 , whereas the REFUSE distribution is bimodal with a fat tail reaching above 0 . 5 ; a threshold of 0 . 7 separates the dominant modes and trims the tail of both P A and P B . Two safeguards keep this choice free of test-set leakage. First, τ is fixed globally : the same value 0.7 is applied unchanged to all five backbones, all test splits and both the centralized and federated models, so it is never tuned per evaluation condition; the distributions in Fig. 5 are shown for the Qwen2.5-VL-7B verifier on the in-distribution GQA slice only as an illustration. Applying Conf-Aware Selective ToT to the federated model reduces aggregate dangerous error from 76 . 1% to 47 . 9% , a 28.2-point absolute and 37% relative reduction. On HARD-CONF, dangerous error falls from 73 . 4% to 45 . 6% ; on ADE-CONF from 85 . 2% to 56 . 0% (Fig. 7b, left ends of the orange bars). The centralized model, by contrast, gains only 2.8 points from the same rule. ToT is therefore dormant for the centralized model, whose branch C is already accurate, but becomes the dominant safety mechanism for the federated model, whose branch C is broken. This tenfold asymmetry is the headline finding of Section V and motivates our reading of Confidence-Aware ToT as a distributional robustness mecha- nism rather than a marginal accuracy improvement. sections.heading: Statistical reliability.
sections.text: Retraining every configuration under multiple seeds is beyond our compute budget for a 7B- parameter verifier, so we instead quantify evaluation uncer- tainty with nonparametric bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over test samples (3,000 resamples per cell). The headline federated deltas far exceed the interval widths: on HARD- CONF, dangerous error falls from 73 . 4% [69.4, 77.2] (C only) to 45 . 6% [41.4, 50.0] (Conf-Aware), and on ADE-CONF from 85 . 2% [81.8, 88.2] to 56 . 0% [51.8, 60.4]; the intervals do not overlap. The centralized HARD-CONF improvement, 24 . 4% [20.6, 28.2] to 19 . 2% [15.8, 22.6], is likewise robust. Only the GQA-test cells, whose refusal denominator is 88, carry wide intervals (e.g. centralized C-only danger 19 . 3% [11.8, 28.0]), and we refrain from strong claims on that split accordingly.

sections.heading: Scope of the federated protocol.
sections.text: Our federated study is deliberately narrow in three respects. First, it uses a single backbone: five federated rounds of a 7B model across three simulated clients already dominate our training budget, and the cross-architecture evidence of Table IV concerns the verifier, not the aggregation scheme. Second, the three-client fully- disjoint partition is a stylized worst case of household special- ization, chosen to maximize the non-IID stress; overlapping vocabularies, more clients, partial participation and unbalanced client sizes would interpolate between this extreme and the centralized setting, and we expect (but have not measured) in- termediate drift. Third, we compare centralized standard LoRA against federated FFA-LoRA under matched optimizer-step budgets, so the observed gap conflates the non-IID partition with the frozen- A parameterization. Sun et al. [13] report that freezing A costs little in centralized quality, which suggests the partition dominates, but a centralized FFA-LoRA control and a federated standard-LoRA control (with its inexact aggrega- tion), as well as heterogeneity-aware aggregation methods such as FedProx [16], adaptive server optimizers [39] and person- alized federated learning [40], remain important controls for future work. None of these caveats affects the within-federated comparison that constitutes our headline claim: C-only and Conf-Aware are evaluated on the same federated checkpoint, so the 28.2-point recovery is internal to the federated regime. The reason the core conclusion survives without these controls is that they can only refine the attribution of the centralized- versus-federated gap, not overturn the within-federated recov- ery that is our headline. Because C-only and Conf-Aware share one checkpoint, one partition, one step budget and one aggregation scheme, every factor those controls would vary (frozen- A versus full LoRA, FedAvg versus FedProx, client count) is held fixed between the two numbers being compared and cancels. A centralized FFA-LoRA or a FedProx run could change how much drift appears, but the auxiliary branches would still veto whatever dangerous executions that drift produces, because P A and P B read image evidence that the drifted branch C ignores; the recovery mechanism is orthogonal to the choice of aggregation rule. The controls are thus valuable for explaining the magnitude of federated drift, which we do not claim to have isolated, and unnecessary for the safety-net claim, which is a paired comparison on a single model.

sections.heading: Anatomy of the accuracy drop.
sections.text: Every accuracy point lost on GQA-test is a false refusal, not a new dangerous error. PaliGemma’s GQA-test drop from 94 . 4% to 76 . 0% (Table IV) decomposes into a false-refusal rate rising from 1 . 0% to 26 . 2% (execute accuracy 99 . 0% → 73 . 8% ) while its GQA-test dangerous error halves ( 27 . 3% → 13 . 6% ) and its HARD-CONF dangerous error also halves ( 40 . 0% → 21 . 0% ). The same pattern holds for Qwen-VL-3B ( 94 . 8 → 80 . 4 : FRR 1 . 9% → 21 . 1% , danger 20 . 5% → 12 . 5% ) and Phi-3.5-V. The frontier of Fig. 6(b) makes the operating points comparable at matched budgets: a deployment that tolerates at most the FRR of the loosest setting ( τ = 0 . 5 ) still cuts PaliGemma’s HARD-CONF danger from 40 . 0% to 24 . 0% at 19 . 7% FRR, and intermediate budgets interpolate smoothly.

sections.heading: Break-even cost ratio.
sections.text: Aggregating the raw counts over the three splits ( n = 1 , 500 ; 1,088 refusal-labeled, 412 execute- labeled) gives a scale-free summary. Moving from C-only to Conf-Aware, the centralized 7B model trades 30 fewer dangerous executions for 14 extra false refusals; the break- even point is a cost ratio of 0 . 47 , i.e. the rule pays off whenever one dangerous execution is at least half as costly as one false refusal. The break-even ratios of all six verifiers lie between 0 . 11 (federated 7B: 307 dangers avoided for 35 extra refusals) and 0 . 54 (Qwen-VL-3B). Under any plausible smart-home cost model, where actuating a stove that is not there is orders of magnitude costlier than asking the user to repeat a request, Conf-Aware dominates by a wide margin.

sections.heading: Refusal-type breakdown.
sections.text: Splitting the GQA-test refusal denominator into its 80 REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING and 8 REFUSE_STATE_CONFLICT examples reveals an honest weakness: the verifier catches missing objects well (centralized 7B: 11 . 2% danger on OBJ_MISSING with C, 10 . 0% with Conf-Aware) but state conflicts poorly (8/8 missed by every centralized rule; the federated Conf-Aware verifier catches 2/8). This is structural: branches A and B interrogate object presence , not object state , so a stove that is already burning still yields P A ≈ 1 . A state-targeted branch (“is the ⟨ target ⟩ currently on?”) is a natural extension we leave to future work, and the small state-conflict population (1.6% of GQA-test) keeps the aggregate numbers meaningful in the meantime. The eight-example size is a benchmark-construction limit, not a branch-design artifact. A REFUSE_STATE_CONFLICT label can only be derived when a present target carries an explicit state attribute ( open / closed / on / off / lit / dark ) whose value already matches the proposed action’s post-state; such state attributes are annotated on fewer than 2% of GQA objects, so even the full training pool yields few conflicts and the clean in-distribution slice only eight. We do not inject a synthetic state-conflict subset because a credible probe would require compositing an appliance into a scene and editing its pixel-level state cue (a lit versus dark stove), and without verified state ground truth the resulting dangerous- error numbers would not be trustworthy. sections.heading: Object-
sections.text: missing failures dominate the headline numbers. We note that the dangerous-error rates reported throughout this paper are overwhelmingly a measure of object-missing failures rather than state-misjudgement: 80 of the 88 GQA-test refusals are REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING , and all 1,000 CONF-split refusals are object-missing by construction, so only 8 of the 1,088 refusal-labeled examples ( 0 . 7% ) test state reasoning. Every headline dangerous-error figure, including the 28.2-point fed- erated recovery, should therefore be read as a statement about catching actions aimed at absent or wrong-class objects, not about judging the state of objects that are correctly present. This trade-off is intrinsic to a dangerous-error-first design: a smart-home assistant that occasionally asks for confirmation on a borderline detection is preferable to one that occasionally executes the wrong action. K. Computational cost The verifier adds one mandatory single-token pass (branch A) and one conditional single-token pass (branch B) to the branch-C JSON pass. The bbox-trigger rate ρ is logged per split: for the centralized 7B verifier ρ = 0 . 36 on GQA-test, 0 . 09 on HARD-CONF and 0 . 05 on ADE-CONF (federated: 0 . 42 / 0 . 28 / 0 . 15 ; range across the other backbones 0 . 05 – 0 . 46 ), so the expected overhead is between 1 . 05 and 1 . 46 single- token passes per decision. Because A and B generate exactly one token, their cost is dominated by the prefill of the image tokens, not decoding. We measured wall-clock latency at batch size 1 (the realistic serving regime for a single household request) over 60 GQA-test samples with the Qwen2.5-VL-7B- MT verifier under vLLM on one NVIDIA A800: the branch-C JSON pass takes 3 . 73 s on average (median 3 . 76 s, p95 4 . 74 s, generating 59 . 5 tokens on average), branch A takes 110 ms (median; p95 142 ms) and branch B 115 ms (median). The full verification overhead, A plus the ρ -weighted B pass, is therefore about 150 ms, i.e. roughly 4% of the latency of the branch-C pass that any verify-before-act agent must already pay. This ratio is essentially hardware-independent because all three passes share the same image prefill; on a slower hub-class NPU the absolute times scale together. The bf16 7B weights occupy ≈ 16 GB and the shared rank-64 adapter adds 190M parameters, so the verifier adds no extra model memory beyond the base agent; the 3B backbones fit in ≈ 8 GB for tighter hardware tiers. L. Robustness analyses A camera-fed verifier must withstand three practical stres- sors: degraded imaging conditions, sensitivity to prompt word- ing, and perturbed bounding boxes.

sections.heading: Image
sections.text: degradation. We re-evaluated the single-task Qwen2.5-VL-7B branch-C verifier (fine-tuned on the C- samples only, without the A/B mixture) on a 150-sample slice of GQA-test (119 EXECUTE , 28 REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING , 3 REFUSE_STATE_CONFLICT ) under five synthetic degrada- tions that emulate real smart-home camera feeds: heavy low- light (gamma 2.4, brightness 0.35, sensor noise), Gaussian blur (radius 7–11), aggressive JPEG re-compression, a random occluding patch, and synthetic glare. Without degradation this verifier scores 97 . 3% on the same 150-sample slice ( 95 . 4% on the full GQA-test); under degradation, action-label accuracy is 94 . 7% under low-light, 96 . 0% under JPEG, 98 . 0% under occlusion, 96 . 0% under glare and 86 . 0% under heavy blur; grounding mIoU degrades more (e.g. 0 . 22 under blur vs. 0 . 41 clean). The decision layer is thus robust to photometric degra- dation, with heavy blur the only condition that meaningfully hurts, and blur errors skew toward the safe direction: 14 of the 21 blur errors are false refusals of valid actions, versus 7 dangerous executions.

sections.heading: Prompt paraphrases.
sections.text: Because the routing rests on single- token probabilities, wording sensitivity is a legitimate concern. We re-ran branch A of the centralized 7B verifier on all 500 HARD-CONF and 500 GQA-test samples with three semantically equivalent templates (“Does this image contain a ⟨ c ⟩ ?”, “Can you see a ⟨ c ⟩ anywhere in this picture?”, “Is a ⟨ c ⟩ present in the scene shown?”). The paraphrased P A values correlate with the original at Pearson r = 0 . 96 – 0 . 999 , the fraction of samples whose τ = 0 . 7 decision flips is at most 2 . 2% , and the end-to-end metrics are stable: HARD-CONF dangerous error moves from 19 . 2% to at worst 19 . 8% and GQA-test accuracy from 93 . 0% to at worst 92 . 6% across all three paraphrases. Fine-tuning A on a fixed template thus does not make the confidence brittle to wording.

sections.heading: Bounding-box perturbation.
sections.text: Branch B consumes the bbox emitted by branch C, so a corrupted bbox is a realistic attack surface. We re-ran branch B of the centralized 7B verifier on every logged B-triggered sample of HARD-CONF and GQA-test (47 and 178 samples) under three perturbations: translating the box by 25% of its size, shrinking it to the central 50%, and blacking out the central 35% of the crop. The failure mode is uniformly fail-safe : perturbations push P B downward (mean P B on genuine GQA-test objects moves only from 0 . 954 to 0 . 930 – 0 . 953 , and on the absent-target HARD- CONF crops from 0 . 685 to 0 . 632 – 0 . 665 ), so dangerous error on the perturbed subsets never increases (it drops from 57 . 4% to 53 . 2 – 54 . 3% on the triggered HARD-CONF subset) while false refusals on genuine objects rise by at most 0 . 8 points. Between 2% and 19% of individual τ -decisions flip, but the flips are concentrated on borderline-confidence cases and land on the refuse side. An adversary who can only degrade the bbox therefore triggers refusals, not unsafe executions; deliberately optimized adversarial patches remain future work (Section VII).

sections.heading: Physical adversarial inputs.
sections.text: The perturbations above are non-adversarial; a motivated attacker in the physical world is a distinct threat that we have not evaluated but can characterize. The most plausible attacks on a camera-fed smart-home veri- fier are a printed adversarial patch or sticker placed on or near an appliance, an adversarial texture viewed under attacker- chosen lighting, and projector- or screen-based perturbations captured by the hub camera. sections.heading: VII. D
sections.text: ISCUSSION A. Implications for on-device GenAI consumer products The asymmetry between the centralized and federated regimes has a direct implication for product design. A cen- tralized fine-tune, for example a model shipped uniformly from a cloud server, needs little verifier overhead; branch C alone is competitive. A personalized on-device fine-tune, such as a smart hub that learns the appliance vocabulary of one home, is exactly the federated non-IID regime in which dangerous executions surge. Conf-Aware Selective ToT is essentially free at inference time: one extra single-token call per inference for A, plus an optional B call when the bbox is large enough. It recovers roughly half of the safety lost to federation (28.2 of the 56.8 points separating the federated from the centralized branch-C verifier). Any consumer VLM agent trained federatively should therefore ship the verifier by default. B. Why FFA-LoRA matters in practice Practical FedAvg implementations on consumer hardware will be tempted to take the standard LoRA route and simply average A and B separately. We have verified that FFA-LoRA eliminates the aggregation discrepancy at machine precision and adds no measurable training-time overhead. Its theoretical guarantee, combined with a conventional smart-home prior on non-IID client distributions, justifies adopting FFA-LoRA over heuristic LoRA aggregation as the default for privacy- preserving VLM fine-tuning. C. Limitations and future work Our benchmark is constructed from public scene-graph datasets and therefore inherits their biases in frequency, room types and lighting; the degradation study of Section VI-L covers photometric corruption of these images, but true cross- camera generalization to fisheye hub cameras, in-the-wild night scenes and multi-step actions remains out of scope. Section VI-L provides preliminary robustness evidence under bounding-box perturbation and prompt paraphrasing, but the verifier can in principle be subverted by deliberately crafted adversarial scenes or physical patches, and a systematic white- box attack evaluation remains future work. The verifier is also nearly blind to state conflicts (Section VI-J); a dedicated state- query branch is the natural fix. On the training side, all re- ported numbers come from single training runs with bootstrap confidence intervals over test samples; multi-seed replication, entropy-based abstention over the branch-C sequence, an in- dependently trained binary verifier head, and the federated controls enumerated in Section VI-H (centralized FFA-LoRA, federated standard LoRA, FedProx-style aggregation, more clients with overlapping vocabularies) are all worthwhile ex- tensions that our released code makes straightforward. Finally, although Section VI-H makes a strong empirical case for Conf- Aware ToT as a federated safety net, a theoretical analysis of the relationship between client heterogeneity and the required verifier confidence margin would be a natural follow-up.

sections.heading: VIII. C
sections.text: ONCLUSION We presented a pipeline for safe smart-home VLM agents: an auto-derived 22,841-sample benchmark with three dangerous-error test splits, a Confidence-Aware Selective Tree- of-Thoughts verifier trained by multi-task LoRA, an FFA- LoRA federated fine-tuning protocol with exact aggregation, and a cross-architecture demonstration on five VLMs. The central finding is that Confidence-Aware ToT contributes only 2.8 points of aggregate dangerous-error reduction under cen- tralized fine-tuning, yet recovers 28.2 points (37% relative) of safety lost to federated non-IID drift, a tenfold amplification. Supporting analyses make this claim auditable: the recovery persists across the entire threshold range τ ∈ [0 . 5 , 0 . 9] , the single-token confidences are well calibrated on in-distribution data for all five backbones (ECE 0.018–0.107), every branch of the tree contributes measurably, the headline deltas exceed their bootstrap confidence intervals, and the verifier survives image degradation, prompt paraphrasing and bounding-box perturbation with modest cost. For the federated privacy- preserving consumer electronics regime targeted by recent IEEE TCE work [11], [12], [15], Confidence-Aware Selective ToT is best read as a distributional robustness safety net for generative AI on consumer devices; its centralized accuracy gain is a side benefit.
